Last quarter we migrated our billing service from MySQL 5.7 to Postgres 15. It took eleven weeks, four weeks longer than planned.

The delay came from one thing we underestimated: 62 stored procedures that nobody on the current team had written. Rewriting them in application code took most of October.

What went well: the dual-write period caught three data mismatches before cutover, and we had zero customer-visible downtime.

What I would do differently: audit the stored procedures in week one, not week five.

text:
After 6 years running a physiotherapy clinic, here is what actually drives repeat visits:

Appointment reminders by WhatsApp, not SMS. Our no-show rate dropped from 18% to 7% within two months of switching.

Explaining the treatment plan in writing at the first visit. Patients who got the printed plan completed 4 more sessions on average.

Neither of these is clinical skill. Both of them changed outcomes more than anything I learned in my last certification.

text:
We reduced our AWS spend from $18,400 to $11,900 per month over one quarter.

The savings broke down as follows: $3,100 from rightsizing eight over-provisioned RDS instances, $2,000 from moving cold S3 data to Glacier, and $1,400 from deleting orphaned EBS volumes that had been detached since 2023.

None of this required an architecture change. It required someone to spend two days reading the bill line by line.

text:
I have been teaching high school physics for 14 years. This year I stopped assigning textbook problem sets for the mechanics unit and replaced them with one project: measure the acceleration due to gravity using anything in your house.

Average test scores went up by roughly 8 points. More interestingly, the students who normally score in the bottom quartile improved the most.

I am not claiming this generalises. It worked for one unit, in one school, with 31 students.

text:
Our support team was drowning at 340 tickets a week. Six months later we are at 190 with the same headcount.

Three changes did most of the work:

We rewrote the top 20 error messages to say what the user should do next. That removed about 60 tickets a week on its own.

We added a status page. Incident-related tickets fell by half during outages.

We let support engineers ship documentation fixes directly, without a review queue.

The remaining 190 are real problems, which is a much better place to be.

text:
Reflections on my first year as an engineering manager.

The hardest part was not the difficult conversations. It was the calendar. I went from four hours of focused work a day to about forty minutes, and it took me six months to stop resenting that.

The most useful habit I built was writing a weekly summary of decisions to the team. It takes twenty minutes on Friday and it has prevented more confusion than any meeting I run.

I still miss writing code. I am told this fades. It has not faded.

label: assisted
text:
We tested three pricing pages over eleven weeks with roughly 9,000 visitors each.

Version A, the original three-tier layout, converted at 2.1%.
Version B, which added an annual toggle, converted at 2.4%.
Version C, which removed the enterprise tier entirely from the page, converted at 3.3%.

We kept version C and moved enterprise to a contact form. Enterprise leads did not drop, which surprised everyone including me.

text:
A note on hiring from someone who has now run 40+ engineering interviews at a small company.

Our take-home assignment had a 46% completion rate. We replaced it with a two-hour paired session on our actual codebase. Completion is effectively 100% and the signal is better, because I get to see how someone asks questions when they are confused.

The cost is my time: two hours per candidate instead of twenty minutes of review. Worth it at our volume. Probably not worth it at 500 candidates a month.

label: assisted
text:
Our restaurant switched to a four-day kitchen week in January. Same total hours, compressed.

Staff turnover in the kitchen for the year: one person, and she moved cities. The year before it was seven.

Food cost and covers are effectively unchanged. Scheduling is harder and Sundays are tight.

I would do it again, but I want to be honest that it made my job more complicated, not less.

text:
Three years of freelance design, summarised for anyone considering it.

Year one revenue: 6.8 lakh. Year two: 14.2 lakh. Year three: 19.5 lakh.

The single biggest change between year one and year two was not skill. It was raising my rate and losing the two clients who took up 60% of my time for 20% of my income.

The hardest month was still August of year two, when two invoices went 90 days overdue at the same time. Keep three months of runway.

text:
We ran a four-week trial of pair programming on our platform team.

Measured outcomes: pull request review time dropped from an average of 19 hours to 3. Defects reaching staging fell from 11 to 4 over the period.

Unmeasured but obvious: two engineers found it exhausting and asked to stop. We now pair on new or risky work only, roughly two days a week.

The compromise is working better than either extreme did.

text:
I rebuilt our warehouse pick paths using the actual order data instead of the layout diagram.

The diagram assumed orders were evenly distributed across the aisles. In reality, 40% of picks came from four bays in aisle 3.

We moved those four bays to the front. Average pick time per order went from 4 minutes 20 seconds to 3 minutes 5 seconds across 1,100 orders measured in November.

The forklift drivers had been saying this for two years.

text:
Notes on writing a 60-page compliance document that people actually read.

We moved every definition to an appendix and put the decision tree on page 2. Reading time in our internal test dropped from 45 minutes to 12, and the number of clarification emails to my team fell from about 15 a week to 3.

The legal review took an extra fortnight because the structure was unfamiliar. That was the price and it was worth paying once.

label: assisted
text:
We tracked how long our new engineers took to make their first production change.

Before: 9 days on average across 11 hires.
After: 2 days across the last 6.

The change was not cultural. We pre-provisioned accounts a week before the start date and wrote a single setup script that replaced a 14-step wiki page.

Boring infrastructure work, measurable result.

text:
After two years of running community meetups in Hyderabad, some numbers.

Average RSVP to attendance ratio: 42%. Providing food raises it to about 60%. Charging 100 rupees raises it to 85%, which is the most counterintuitive thing I have learned.

Speaker recruitment is the real constraint, not venue or budget. I now ask every attendee who asks a good question whether they would speak next time. Roughly one in ten says yes.

label: assisted
text:
Our churn analysis, written up plainly because I could not find one of these when I needed it.

Monthly churn was 4.1%. We segmented by onboarding completion and found that users who connected a data source in week one churned at 1.8%, and those who did not churned at 9.4%.

So we made connecting a data source the only thing on the first screen. Three months later, blended churn is 3.0%.

One variable, one screen, one clear result. Most of our other experiments did nothing.

Six months into using an AI assistant for code review at work, here is what I have observed on our team of nine.

It catches null handling and off-by-one issues reliably. It has never once caught a problem that came from misunderstanding the product requirement, which is where our real bugs come from.

Review time is down. Review quality is roughly unchanged. I would not remove it and I would not trust it as the only reviewer.

text:
We surveyed 212 customers who cancelled in the last year and actually read every response.

The most common reason was not price, which is what our sales team assumed. It was that the person who championed us left the company. That appeared in 38% of responses.

We now do quarterly check-ins with a second stakeholder on every account above a certain size. Too early to say whether it works.

label: assisted
text:
Documenting our incident from March 14th publicly, because we said we would.

A schema migration added a NOT NULL column with a default to a 40 million row table, which locked writes for 6 minutes 40 seconds during peak hours.

We knew this was a risk on our old Postgres version. The migration passed review because the reviewer assumed we were on version 11 or later, where the behaviour changed. We were on 10.

We have pinned a version check into the migration linter.

text:
What changed when our sales team stopped using a script.

Call length on first meetings dropped by an average of 11 minutes. Conversion to second meeting went from 31% to 34%, which is within noise for our volume, so I will not claim it as a win.

What is clearly true: rep satisfaction went up and two people who were about to quit stayed. Sometimes the metric that moves is not the one on the dashboard.

text:
Five years of running a two-person consultancy, honestly summarised.

About 70% of our revenue has come from four clients. That is a concentration risk we have failed to fix every year.

Our best lead source has been former colleagues, not content, not conferences, not cold outreach. We spent 2023 trying to change that and it did not work.

I am writing this down mostly so that I read it before we spend another year on it.

label: assisted
text:
We replaced our nightly batch job with incremental processing.

Runtime went from 3 hours 40 minutes to a steady stream with a 90 second lag. That was the goal and we hit it.

What we did not anticipate: three downstream reports assumed the data was frozen between midnight and 4am, and two of them started producing inconsistent totals. Finding those took another two weeks.

If you do this, inventory who reads your outputs before you change how they are produced.
